title: Problem-Solver Studio
goal: Your kid takes something that keeps bugging them, like the water bottle they lose every week, and solves it for good. They find out why it keeps happening, get every idea out, build the simplest fix, test it for real and make a better version.
need: A problem that keeps coming back
Paper, a pencil and a timer
Whatever's around the house: hooks, tape, boxes, labels
A few days to test it

academics.subject: Science
academics.text: testing an idea and changing one thing

academics.subject: Writing
academics.text: saying exactly what the problem is

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: You're the coach, not the problem-solver. Let them pick something that truly annoys them, even if it isn't what annoys you. Slow them down at 'why', because kids want to jump straight to fixing. And keep it light: a test that fails is the most useful part.

plan.what: Pick the problem and find the because (Steps 1 and 2).
Get every idea out, then pick one and build it (Steps 3 and 4).

troubleshoot.q: The problem seems small to me
troubleshoot.a: Small is perfect. A hook for a water bottle teaches the same thinking as a big fix, and they can finish it this week.

troubleshoot.q: It's a problem the whole family shares
troubleshoot.a: Have your kid interview everyone it affects first, one question each: what happens, when, and what would make it easy? Now the fix has to work for all of them, not just for your kid.

troubleshoot.q: Their fix depends on someone else
troubleshoot.a: Ask 'What part of this is yours?' Putting up a divider works. 'My sister should stop' doesn't.
Good, now you've got something to work with. Ask what happened right before it failed, and change one thing.

lesson.text: Most fixes fail because they go after the part you can see. A good fix goes after the reason it keeps happening, and it still works on a tired day.
lesson.before: I'll try harder to remember my water bottle.

model.line: I lose my water bottle about three times a week.
I put it down wherever I am when I walk in.
A hook right by the door, at my height.
Four days, lost it once. Moved the hook closer.

lesson.modelNote: Trying harder lasts about a day. The hook keeps working when they're tired, because there's nothing to remember.

steps.title: Pick what keeps bugging you
steps.why: The best problems are small, real and happen all the time.
steps.kid: Your kid picks something that happens at least a few times a week, using the Everyday problems card in the Studio Toolkit at the end of the guide or an idea of their own. They say it in one specific sentence.
steps.you: Let them choose, even if you'd pick something else. If the sentence is vague, ask them to show you exactly what happens.
ask: How often does this really happen?
steps.tip: 'My sister is annoying' can't be worked on. 'Her stuff ends up on my bed' can.

levels.explore: Pick one problem and say it in one sentence.
levels.develop: Pick one that happens at least three times a week, and count it for two days.
levels.extend: Pick one that affects other people too, and write down who and how.

steps.title: Find the because
steps.why: Fix the wrong thing and it comes right back.
steps.kid: Your kid watches the problem happen and uses the Why questions card to dig into it. Then they finish this sentence: 'When I ___, I often ___, because ___.' That last blank is the whole point.
steps.you: Keep asking why, and hold them back from fixing it yet. Watch it happen with them, and tell them what you notice.
ask: What happens right before it goes wrong?
steps.tip: Watch it happen instead of trying to remember it. Things look different when you're paying attention.

levels.explore: Finish the sentence with your because.
levels.develop: Finish the sentence and find two different causes.
levels.extend: Interview everyone the problem affects, then write down the causes and one limit you can't change.

steps.title: Get every idea out
steps.why: The first idea is rarely the good one.
steps.kid: Your kid sets a timer for five minutes and writes or draws every idea they can, using the Idea starters card when they get stuck. Silly and impossible ones count. When the timer goes, they circle the ones that could really happen.
steps.you: Add a few terrible ideas of your own. No one says 'that won't work' until the timer stops.
ask: What would you do if time and money didn't matter?
Can you combine two of these?
steps.tip: 'Hire a robot butler' really means 'I want the boring part to happen by itself.' Ask what that could look like in real life.

levels.explore: Come up with four ideas, out loud or in drawings.
levels.develop: Come up with six to eight, and circle the ones that could really happen.
levels.extend: Come up with ten or more, then combine two into something new.

steps.title: Pick one and build it
steps.why: The best idea is the one you'll still do when you're tired.
steps.kid: Your kid runs their circled ideas through Tired-day tests card and picks one. Then they fill in My fix at the end of the guide and build it for real: a hook, a label, a box, a checklist, an alarm.
steps.you: Steer them toward simple, and help with anything that needs a drill. Otherwise let it be a bit wonky. Help them pick something to count.
ask: What could you build in ten minutes?
Will it work on a tired day?
steps.tip: Put the fix exactly where the problem happens. A checklist in a drawer doesn't check anything.

levels.explore: Pick one idea and build the simplest version.
levels.develop: Pick one, list what you need and how you'll count whether it worked, then build it.
levels.extend: Build two small versions, and decide how you'll test which one wins.

steps.title: Test it and make Version 2
steps.why: The first version almost never works. That's what it's for.
steps.kid: Your kid uses their fix for a few days and counts what they said they'd count. Then they work out what went wrong, change one thing and try again. When it works, they show someone else how it works.
steps.you: Don't remind them, because reminding ruins the test. Check in after a few days and ask what they noticed.
ask: Did it work on the tired day?
What one change would help the most?
steps.tip: Count before and after, even roughly. Finding your shoes in ten seconds is very satisfying.

levels.explore: Try it once, change one thing and tell someone what you changed.
levels.develop: Test it for two or three days, count the results and make two changes.
levels.extend: Test it for five days, rate each day and make a guide someone else could follow.

items.ask: Will you still do it next week?

conclusion.headline: One less thing bugging them, and they fixed it themselves.
conclusion.text: The real sign comes later, when something new starts bugging them. If they ask 'Why does that keep happening?' instead of complaining, or quietly put up another hook, they've started to see problems as something they can work on.
conclusion.celebrate: The first time it works on a tired day, say: 'You built that, and it's still working.'
extensions: Solve a shared family problem the same way, like what's for supper
Turn your fix into a seven-day challenge and track it
Make a list of three small systems that make life easier
Spot a fix someone else made, like a hook or a label, and work out the problem it solved

signs: They ask why something keeps happening
They try a small fix before complaining
They change one thing and try again
makeItReal: The next time someone in the family complains about the same thing twice, ask: 'What's the because?'
